cards.title: Top of the Ladder
cards.instruction: Carry yourself as the highest-status person present. Treat questions as requests for your approval.

cards.title: One Thing Leads to Another
cards.instruction: Use each small problem to justify solving a broader, more disruptive problem.

beats.speaker: A
beats.text: I'll decide how we handle this. This dripping tap is our chance to replace the whole sink.

beats.speaker: B
beats.text: It only needs a washer. I've bought one.

beats.speaker: A
beats.text: You can question the details after my decision. Excellent. We'll fit it while the sink's out and replace that swollen worktop.

beats.speaker: B
beats.text: The worktop runs under every cupboard.

beats.speaker: A
beats.text: Then we'll empty the kitchen. With the cupboards out, we can finally fix the layout.

cardFidelity.evidence: A1 decides and A3 restricts questions, but A5 ordinary renovation proposal does not sustain permission as the means of expanding work.

responseLogic.evidence: B2 washer solution causes A3 incorporating it into sink removal and worktop replacement; B4 continuous worktop causes A5 kitchen removal.

relationship.evidence: B2 has bought the small fix and B4 identifies a structural dependency, credibly trying to contain scope.

heightening.evidence: B4 dependency becomes A5 reason to empty all cupboards and redesign the layout.

specificity.evidence: A1 dripping tap, A3 swollen worktop and B4 its extent establish concrete stages of increasing disruption.

brevityWit.evidence: A5 finally-fix-the-layout follows B4 cupboard dependency, but A3 stock restriction slows the practical reasoning.
